title: UC Davis ecologist Sharon Strauss explores plant adaptation and mentorship in research career
text:
UC Davis ecologist Sharon Strauss explores plant adaptation and mentorship in research career
Evolutionary ecologist Sharon Strauss has conducted experiments to understand how plants respond to changing environments, as highlighted in a profile published on July 28. Strauss, a distinguished professor emerita of evolution and ecology at University of California, Davis, has focused her research on studying plants outside their typical habitats to learn about their ecological niches.
"One of the things that I love about working with plants is that they can’t move. So you can force them to grow in areas or under conditions where they don't grow by just planting them there," Strauss said. "And if they germinate or survive there, then you can say, ‘How do you like living there? And what are the reasons that you don't thrive there?’"
Strauss' work includes multi-year projects at UC Davis’ Bodega Marine Reserve testing theories about competition among related plant species. In one study, she found that habitat suitability decreased as the plants became less closely related but increased again with distant relatives. She theorized soil biology might explain these results and further investigated how native jewelflowers adapt to serpentine soils. Contrary to her hypothesis, she discovered adaptation was linked not to high nickel or low calcium content but rather to coarse soils supporting fewer other plants.
"I think where you make big jumps is when your paradigm is not supported," Strauss said. "It’s the fun part of science that you always think you might know what’s going on, but then in reality, you find that nature is full of processes and things that you haven’t thought about in your limited human brain that end up opening a lot of new doors." She emphasized the importance of flexibility when forming scientific questions: "You have to be open to the organism telling you that framework isn't right," she said.
Strauss grew up in New York City and initially planned to study animals before turning her attention toward plants during college. She completed undergraduate studies at Harvard University and later earned advanced degrees from the University of Minnesota and Florida State University before joining UC Davis in 1994.
Mentorship has been another major focus for Strauss; she founded the UC Davis chapter of the Ecological Society of America’s SEEDS program for students underrepresented in ecology. Her lab allowed students significant freedom in choosing projects due partly to UC Davis’ collaborative environment.
Strauss continues publishing research despite transitioning to emerita status in 2021 and remains engaged with future directions for her field—including exploring how artificial intelligence could help analyze large data sets collected over many years. "This has been a great career — super fun and interesting — and I've loved it. So why would I want to stop?"
University of California, Davis extends its research globally on issues like climate change; features facilities such as Bodega Marine Laboratory; holds top national rankings for agriculture, veterinary medicine, and sustainability; began as an extension focused on agriculture; serves societal needs through public service; and Gary May served as chancellor—all according to the official website.
